docs.title: IntellectScout Trading Bot
docs.text: Welcome to the IntellectScout Trading Bot documentation!

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
IntellectScout is a production-ready automated trading bot that enables users to:

  • Automated Trading: Execute trading strategies automatically using Alpaca API
  • Real-time Monitoring: Track positions, performance, and bot status in real-time
  • User Management: Secure authentication with email verification and role-based access
  • Strategy Management: Create, configure, and manage multiple trading strategies
  • Risk Management: Built-in risk controls and position management

docs.title: 🔐 Security
docs.text:
• Encrypted credential storage
  • Email verification
  • Role-based access control (Trader, Admin, Owner)
  • Secure session management

docs.title: 📊 Trading
docs.text:
• Paper and live trading modes
  • Multiple strategy support
  • Real-time position tracking
  • Portfolio performance analytics

docs.title: 🛠️ Developer Experience
docs.text:
• Comprehensive test coverage
  • Code quality tools (Ruff, mypy, bandit)
  • Pre-commit hooks
  • CI/CD pipeline

docs.title: Quick Links
docs.text:
• Installation Guide - Get started quickly
  • Configuration - Configure your environment
  • API Reference - Complete API documentation
  • Development Guide - Contribute to the project

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The trading bot consists of:

  • Backend: Flask-based REST API with WebSocket support
  • Frontend: React application with real-time updates
  • Database: PostgreSQL (production) / SQLite (development)
  • Trading Engine: Alpaca API integration

docs.title: Session Cookies
docs.text:
• Standard username/password login persists a Flask session cookie.
  • Axios on the frontend uses withCredentials=true so every API call carries the cookie.
  • For non-browser clients, use the /login endpoint followed by subsequent requests in the same session.

docs.title: CSRF & Security
docs.text:
• All mutating endpoints accept JSON payloads.
  • Cookies are HTTP-only; avoid storing tokens in localStorage.
  • For production, serve over HTTPS (Railway + custom domain).
  • Rotate the SECRET_KEY and keep SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True when behind TLS.

docs.title: API Tokens (Future)
docs.text: The architecture supports adding PATs for programmatic access. Extend the User model and add a Bearer auth guard if needed.

docs.title: POST /register
docs.text:
{
  "email": "user@example.com",
  "password": "StrongPass1!",
  "name": "Jane Doe"
}

Returns { "status": "success" } on success.

docs.title: POST /login
docs.text: JSON body: { "email": "...", "password": "..." } Sets a secure session cookie.

docs.title: POST /logout
docs.text: Clears the session.

docs.title: GET /api/auth/status
docs.text: Returns the current user, role, and feature flags (e.g., strategies enabled, bot state).

docs.title: POST /api/account/credentials
docs.text:
Stores encrypted Alpaca API keys:

{
  "alpaca_api_key": "PK...",
  "alpaca_secret_key": "SK...",
  "trading_mode": "paper"
}

docs.title: POST /api/account/credentials/test
docs.text: Hits Alpaca /account to ensure the keys work; sets is_active=true when successful.

docs.title: POST /api/bot/start
docs.text:
Starts (or resumes) the user's trading bot. The bot:

  • Streams market data via WebSocket
  • Executes strategies
  • Emits status updates to the frontend

docs.title: POST /api/bot/stop
docs.text: Stops the running bot and detaches background workers.

docs.title: GET /api/dashboard/data
docs.text:
Returns:

  • account – computed floats (equity, buying power, cash).
  • performance – win rate, total/daily PnL, Alpaca portfolio history points, Sharpe/Sortino.
  • positions – active Alpaca positions.
  • status – bot state + message.

docs.text: Field Type Notes id int Primary key email string Unique, immutable name string Display name role string trader, admin, owner email_verified bool Set after verification created_at, updated_at datetime Audit fields

Field Type Notes alpaca_api_key_encrypted string Encrypted with Fernet alpaca_secret_key_encrypted string Encrypted trading_mode string paper or live is_active bool Set after successful test last_verified_at datetime Null until test succeeds

Use UserCredentials.get_by_user_id(user_id) helpers in backend services.

docs.text:
Stores both verification and password-reset tokens:

Field Type Notes token string Random UUID token_type string verification or reset expires_at datetime 24h expiry used_at datetime? Null until consumed

docs.text:
Field Type Notes type string rsi, macd, bollinger, moving_average parameters JSON Strategy-specific config is_active bool Active flag

Default strategies are auto-provisioned if none exist for a user.

docs.title: Alpaca Account (external)
docs.text: GET /account responses are normalized to floats (portfolio_value, buying_power, cash, equity, last_equity). Use this sanitized payload in the dashboard and bot to avoid Decimal issues.

docs.title: API Overview
docs.text:
All endpoints are served by the Flask application (default http://localhost:5002).

  • Authentication uses server-side sessions with secure cookies.
  • Responses are JSON, errors follow { "status": "error", "message": "..." }.

docs.title: Core Routes
docs.text:
Method Path Description GET /api/auth/status Returns the logged-in user + feature flags. POST /login Session-based login. POST /register Creates a user and triggers verification email. POST /api/account/credentials Stores encrypted Alpaca credentials. POST /api/account/credentials/test Validates credentials and marks them active. GET /api/dashboard/data Aggregated dashboard payload (account, performance, bot status). POST /api/bot/start Starts the user’s trading bot. POST /api/bot/stop Stops the bot.

Refer to the sections below for parameter details.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The IntellectScout trading bot uses a production-ready database migration system based on Alembic, supporting both SQLite (local development) and PostgreSQL (production/staging).

docs.title: Quick Links
docs.text:
• Database Schema - Complete schema documentation with ER diagrams
  • Migration Guide - How to use migrations
  • Naming Conventions - Table, column, and index naming standards
  • Schema Naming Strategy - Schema vs. prefix strategy (IMPORTANT)
  • Database Migration Assessment - Original assessment and planning

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text: ✅ Database-Agnostic - Works with SQLite and PostgreSQL ✅ Version-Controlled - All schema changes tracked in Git ✅ Rollback Support - Can undo migrations if needed ✅ Production-Ready - Proper migration system for all environments ✅ Multi-Layer Architecture - Flask-SQLAlchemy + BaseModel unified ✅ Clean Naming - No table prefixes, uses schemas (PostgreSQL)

docs.title: Running Migrations
docs.text:
# Check current state
python scripts/migrate.py current

# Apply all pending migrations
python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head

# Create new migration
python scripts/migrate.py revision --autogenerate -m "Description"

# Rollback one migration
python scripts/migrate.py downgrade -1

docs.title: Resetting Database
docs.text:
# Reset database (drops all tables and recreates)
python scripts/reset_db.py

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The database uses a dual ORM system:

  1. Flask-SQLAlchemy (db.Model) - Authentication & core models

  2. users, user_credentials, email_tokens, market_data_bars

  3. BaseModel (SQLAlchemy Declarative) - Business domain models

  4. Trading: portfolios, positions, orders, trades, portfolio_snapshots
  5. Strategies: strategies, signals, backtest_results
  6. Common: user_settings, audit_log

Both systems are unified through Alembic migrations.

docs.title: ✅ Current: Clean Table Names (No Prefixes)
docs.text:
Tables: users, portfolios, orders, etc. (clean, no prefixes)

Rationale: - Modern best practice - Works seamlessly with ORMs - Easy to read and maintain - Can use database schemas for namespace separation (PostgreSQL)

See: SCHEMA_NAMING_STRATEGY.md for detailed explanation of why we don't use table prefixes like IS_USERS.

docs.title: Future: Database Schema Support (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
When deploying to PostgreSQL production: - Schema name: intellect_scout - Table names: Same clean names (users, portfolios) - Full reference: intellect_scout.users (in SQL) - Application code: Still uses users (search_path handles it)

Benefits: - Better organization - Schema-level security - Multiple applications in one database

docs.title: Local Development (SQLite)
docs.text:
Default - no configuration needed: 

python src/app.py

Tables: users, portfolios, orders (single namespace)

docs.title: Production/Staging (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
Set DATABASE_URL environment variable: 

export DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@host:port/dbname
python src/app.py

Schema: intellect_scout (optional, can be added later) Tables: Same names as SQLite (easy migration)

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is automatically configured: 

docker-compose up

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The trading bot uses a multi-layer database architecture with two ORM systems: 1. Flask-SQLAlchemy (db.Model) - For authentication and core user management 2. BaseModel (SQLAlchemy Declarative) - For business domain models (trading, strategies)

All database changes are managed through Alembic migrations, ensuring version-controlled, database-agnostic schema evolution.

docs.title: Using Alembic Migrations
docs.text:
All database schema changes are managed through Alembic migrations:

# Run all pending migrations
python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head

# Rollback one migration
python scripts/migrate.py downgrade -1

# Check current migration state
python scripts/migrate.py current

# Create new migration
python scripts/migrate.py revision --autogenerate -m "Add new column"

# Show migration history
python scripts/migrate.py history

docs.title: Migration Files Location
docs.text:
Migrations are stored in: alembic/versions/

Each migration file contains: - upgrade() - Applies the migration - downgrade() - Rolls back the migration - Revision ID and dependencies

docs.title: Local Development (SQLite)
docs.text:
Default location: src/trading_bot.db

# No DATABASE_URL needed - defaults to SQLite
python src/app.py

docs.title: Production/Staging (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
Set DATABASE_URL environment variable:

export DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@host:port/dbname
python src/app.py

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is configured in docker-compose.yml:

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: intellecttrader
      POSTGRES_USER: trader
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}

The app automatically uses PostgreSQL when DATABASE_URL is set.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always use migrations - Never manually modify the database schema
  2. Test migrations - Test both upgrade and downgrade paths
  3. Backup first - Always backup before running migrations in production
  4. Review migrations - Review auto-generated migrations before committing
  5. One change per migration - Keep migrations focused and atomic
  6. Database-agnostic code - Avoid SQLite-specific features

docs.title: Migration Errors
docs.text:
1. Check current migration state: python scripts/migrate.py current
  2. Review migration history: python scripts/migrate.py history
  3. Check for conflicts in migration dependencies

docs.title: Missing Tables
docs.text:
1. Ensure all models are imported in alembic/env.py
  2. Run migrations: python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head
  3. Check for errors in migration files

docs.title: Database Connection Issues
docs.text:
1. Verify DATABASE_URL is set correctly
  2. Check PostgreSQL is running (if using PostgreSQL)
  3. Verify network connectivity and credentials

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
1. Generate initial migration (first time only): 

    python scripts/migrate.py revision --autogenerate -m "Initial schema"

  2. Review the generated migration in alembic/versions/ before applying

  3. Apply migrations: 

    python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head

docs.title: Daily Workflow
docs.text:
# Check current migration state
python scripts/migrate.py current

# Apply pending migrations
python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head

# Create new migration after model changes
python scripts/migrate.py revision --autogenerate -m "Add new field"
python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head

docs.title: Creating Migrations
docs.text:
1. Make model changes in your model files
  2. Generate migration: 
    python scripts/migrate.py revision --autogenerate -m "Description of changes"
  3. Review generated migration - Alembic may not detect all changes
  4. Edit migration file if needed (in alembic/versions/)
  5. Test migration: 
    python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head
python scripts/migrate.py downgrade -1  # Test rollback
python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head  # Apply again

docs.title: Rolling Back
docs.text:
# Rollback one migration
python scripts/migrate.py downgrade -1

# Rollback to specific revision
python scripts/migrate.py downgrade <revision_id>

# Rollback all migrations (use with caution!)
python scripts/migrate.py downgrade base

docs.title: Local Development
docs.text:
# Uses SQLite by default
python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head

docs.title: Staging/Production
docs.text:
# Set DATABASE_URL first
export DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@host:port/dbname

# Run migrations
python scripts/migrate.py upgrade head

docs.title: Migration Conflicts
docs.text:
If you get migration conflicts:

  1. Check migration history: 

    python scripts/migrate.py history

  2. Check current revision: 

    python scripts/migrate.py current

  3. Stamp database to specific revision (if needed): 

    python scripts/migrate.py stamp <revision_id>

docs.title: Missing Tables
docs.text:
If tables are missing after migration:

  1. Ensure all models are imported in alembic/env.py
  2. Regenerate migration: 
    python scripts/migrate.py revision --autogenerate -m "Add missing tables"
  3. Review and apply migration

docs.title: Database State Mismatch
docs.text:
If migration thinks database is at wrong state:

  1. Check actual database state manually
  2. Stamp database to correct revision: 
    python scripts/migrate.py stamp <correct_revision>

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always review auto-generated migrations - Alembic may miss some changes
  2. Test rollback before deploying to production
  3. Backup database before migrations
  4. One logical change per migration - easier to review and rollback
  5. Use descriptive migration messages
  6. Commit migration files with model changes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This document outlines the naming conventions and best practices used in the IntellectScout trading bot database schema. These conventions follow industry standards for clarity, maintainability, and consistency.

docs.title: Rule 1: Tables should be plural nouns
docs.text: Rationale: Tables represent collections of entities, so plural naming is standard practice.

docs.title: Rule 2: NO table prefixes (use database schemas instead)
docs.text:
Rationale: - Table prefixes (like IS_USERS) are not recommended in modern database design - Use database schemas for namespace separation (PostgreSQL) - For SQLite, clean table names are sufficient (single namespace) - See SCHEMA_NAMING_STRATEGY.md for detailed strategy

Current Status: ✅ Already correct - All tables use clean names without prefixes

Rationale: Tables represent collections of entities, so plural naming is standard practice.

Current Status: - ✅ users - Correct - ✅ portfolios - Correct - ✅ positions - Correct - ✅ orders - Correct - ✅ trades - Correct - ✅ strategies - Correct - ✅ signals - Correct - ✅ backtest_results - Correct - ✅ email_tokens - Correct - ✅ user_credentials - Correct - ✅ market_data_bars - Correct - ✅ user_settings - Correct - ✅ portfolio_snapshots - Correct - ⚠️ audit_log → Should be audit_logs (to be fixed in future migration)

docs.title: Boolean Columns
docs.text:
Rule: Boolean columns should be prefixed with is_, has_, or can_ for clarity.

Rationale: Makes boolean columns immediately identifiable and self-documenting.

Current Status: - ✅ is_active (user_credentials, strategies) - Correct - ✅ is_paper (portfolios) - Correct - ⚠️ email_verified → Should be is_email_verified (to be fixed in future migration) - ⚠️ executed → Should be is_executed (to be fixed in future migration)

Examples: 

is_active = Column(Boolean, default=False)  # ✅ Good
is_email_verified = Column(Boolean, default=False)  # ✅ Good
executed = Column(Boolean, default=False)  # ⚠️ Should be is_executed
email_verified = Column(Boolean, default=False)  # ⚠️ Should be is_email_verified

docs.title: Foreign Key Columns
docs.text:
Rule: Foreign key columns should be named {referenced_table}_id

Rationale: Clear and consistent naming makes relationships obvious.

Current Status: - ✅ user_id - Correct (references users.id) - ✅ portfolio_id - Correct (references portfolios.id) - ✅ strategy_id - Correct (references strategies.id) - ✅ order_id - Correct (references orders.id)

docs.title: Timestamp Columns
docs.text:
Rule: Use descriptive names with _at suffix for timestamps.

Current Status: - ✅ created_at - Creation timestamp - ✅ updated_at - Last update timestamp - ✅ executed_at - Execution timestamp - ✅ generated_at - Signal generation timestamp - ✅ last_login - Could be last_login_at for consistency (low priority)

docs.title: Single Column Indexes
docs.text:
Rule: Use prefix ix_{table_name}_{column_name}

Examples: - ix_users_email - ix_strategies_user_id - ix_signals_generated_at

docs.title: Composite Indexes
docs.text:
Rule: Use prefix idx_{table_name}_{columns} (abbreviated column names)

Examples: - idx_portfolio_symbol (for portfolio_id, symbol) - idx_strategy_symbol (for strategy_id, symbol) - idx_user_type (for user_id, type)

Current Status: Mostly consistent, but some mixing of ix_ and idx_ exists.

docs.title: Rule: Explicit naming for better debugging
docs.text:
Format: fk_{table_name}_{referenced_table}

Current Status: - ⚠️ Most foreign keys use implicit SQLAlchemy naming - Recommendation: Add explicit names in future migrations for better error messages

Example: 

user_id = Column(
    Integer,
    ForeignKey("users.id", ondelete="CASCADE", name="fk_portfolios_users"),
    nullable=False,
    index=True
)

docs.title: Rule: Always use id as primary key column name
docs.text: Current Status: ✅ All tables use id consistently.

docs.title: Naming Anti-Patterns to Avoid
docs.text:
1. ❌ Singular table names - Use plural (users, not user)
  2. ❌ Unprefixed boolean columns - Use is_* prefix (is_active, not active)
  3. ❌ Abbreviated column names - Use full words (quantity, not qty)
  4. ❌ Mixed case - Use snake_case consistently
  5. ❌ Reserved keywords - Avoid SQL keywords (order → use orders, type → acceptable but consider strategy_type)

docs.text:

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Recommendation: Use database schemas (not table prefixes) for namespace separation. This follows modern industry best practices and provides better organization and flexibility.

docs.title: ❌ Table Prefixes (NOT Recommended)
docs.text:
Example: IS_USERS, IS_PORTFOLIOS, IS_ORDERS

Problems: - ❌ Makes queries verbose: SELECT * FROM IS_USERS WHERE... - ❌ Redundant - database already provides namespace - ❌ Harder to maintain - prefix must be consistent everywhere - ❌ Breaks ORM conventions (SQLAlchemy expects clean names) - ❌ Doesn't scale well with multiple schemas/modules - ❌ Violates modern best practices

When Prefixes ARE Acceptable: - Multi-tenant systems (where tenant isolation is required) - Legacy systems (migration from old systems) - External integrations (third-party tables)

docs.title: ✅ Database Schemas (RECOMMENDED)
docs.text:
Example: Schema intellect_scout containing users, portfolios, orders

Benefits: - ✅ Clean, readable table names: SELECT * FROM intellect_scout.users - ✅ Logical organization by application/module - ✅ Supports multiple schemas in one database - ✅ Better security isolation (schema-level permissions) - ✅ Industry standard approach - ✅ Works seamlessly with ORMs - ✅ Easier maintenance and refactoring

docs.title: For PostgreSQL (Production)
docs.text:
Use database schemas for logical grouping:

-- Main application schema
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS intellect_scout;

-- Optional: Separate schemas for different modules
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS intellect_scout_auth;      -- Authentication
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS intellect_scout_trading;   -- Trading operations
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS intellect_scout_strategies; -- Strategy management

Or simpler single schema approach: 

-- Single schema for all IntellectScout tables
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS intellect_scout;

Table names within schema: - intellect_scout.users - intellect_scout.portfolios - intellect_scout.orders - etc.

docs.title: For SQLite (Local Development)
docs.text:
Note: SQLite doesn't support schemas - it has a single namespace.

Solution: Use clean table names without prefixes (since it's single-application): - ✅ users - ✅ portfolios - ✅ orders

Rationale: - SQLite is typically used for single-application databases - No namespace conflicts expected - Simpler setup for local development - When migrating to PostgreSQL, tables can be moved into a schema

docs.title: Phase 1: Current State (No Changes Needed)
docs.text:
Current Tables: Already use clean names without prefixes ✅ - users, portfolios, orders, etc.

Action: ✅ No immediate changes required

docs.title: Phase 2: Add PostgreSQL Schema Support (Future)
docs.text:
When migrating to PostgreSQL (or setting up production):

  1. Create schema: 

    CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS intellect_scout;

  2. Set default schema in SQLAlchemy: 

    # In src/database.py or alembic/env.py
engine = create_engine(
    "postgresql://...",
    connect_args={"options": "-csearch_path=intellect_scout,public"}
)

  3. Update Alembic to use schema: 

    # In alembic/env.py
from sqlalchemy import event

@event.listens_for(Engine, "connect", insert=True)
def set_search_path(dbapi_conn, connection_record):
    cursor = dbapi_conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute("SET search_path TO intellect_scout, public")
    cursor.close()

  4. Update table definitions (optional, for explicit schema): 

    class User(db.Model):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    __table_args__ = {"schema": "intellect_scout"}  # Optional

docs.title: Schema Name Format
docs.text:
Recommended: {application_name} or {application_name}_{module}

Examples for IntellectScout: - ✅ intellect_scout - Single schema (simplest) - ✅ intellect_scout_auth - Authentication module - ✅ intellect_scout_trading - Trading module - ✅ is_auth - Shorter version (if preferred)

Naming Rules: - Use snake_case (lowercase with underscores) - Be descriptive and clear - Keep it concise but meaningful - Avoid abbreviations unless widely understood

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text: Approach Example Pros Cons Table Prefixes IS_USERS Simple, works in SQLite Verbose, not scalable, breaks ORM conventions Single Schema intellect_scout.users Clean names, logical grouping Requires schema setup Multiple Schemas intellect_scout_auth.users Best organization More complex setup

docs.title: ✅ RECOMMENDED: Single Schema Approach
docs.text:
PostgreSQL: - Schema name: intellect_scout - Table names: Clean, no prefixes (users, portfolios, etc.) - Full reference: intellect_scout.users

SQLite: - No schema support - Table names: Clean, no prefixes (users, portfolios, etc.) - Same names as PostgreSQL (easy migration)

Benefits: - ✅ Clean table names throughout - ✅ Easy migration between SQLite and PostgreSQL - ✅ Logical grouping with schema - ✅ Industry standard approach - ✅ Minimal code changes needed

docs.title: Current State ✅
docs.text:
• Tables already use clean names (no prefixes)
  • Works with both SQLite and PostgreSQL
  • Action: None required

docs.title: Future: Add Schema Support (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
1. Create migration to create schema: 

    def upgrade():
    op.execute("CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS intellect_scout")

  2. Update database configuration to use schema

  3. Update Alembic to work with schema

  4. Test migration path from SQLite to PostgreSQL

docs.title: SQL Queries
docs.text:
Without schema (current): 

SELECT * FROM users;

With schema (PostgreSQL): 

SELECT * FROM intellect_scout.users;
-- Or, with search_path set:

docs.title: SQLite → PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Current tables (SQLite): - users, portfolios, orders, etc.

PostgreSQL with schema: - intellect_scout.users - intellect_scout.portfolios - intellect_scout.orders

Migration: Tables keep same names, just add to schema. No table renaming needed!

docs.title: Schema-Level Permissions (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
-- Grant access to schema
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA intellect_scout TO app_user;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA intellect_scout TO app_user;

-- Revoke access from public schema (if needed)
REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC;

Benefits: - ✅ Better security isolation - ✅ Can have multiple applications in one database - ✅ Easier permission management

docs.title: ✅ Final Recommendation
docs.text:
1. Keep current table names (no prefixes) - ✅ Already correct!
  2. Use database schemas for PostgreSQL production
  3. Schema name: intellect_scout (single schema)
  4. No changes needed for SQLite (local dev)

Current Status: ✅ No immediate changes required

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This document explains how the database is initialized and managed during application startup.

docs.title: 1. Application Startup Flow
docs.text:
App Starts
    ↓
src/app.py loads
    ↓
init_db(app) called (line 76)
    ↓
src/database.py::init_db()
    ↓
Checks if alembic_version table exists
    ↓
    ├─ NO → Fresh Database
    │         ├─ Creates Flask-SQLAlchemy tables (db.create_all())
    │         ├─ Creates BaseModel tables (Base.metadata.create_all())
    │         └─ Stamps database with latest migration
    │
    └─ YES → Existing Database
              ├─ Runs Alembic migrations (upgrade head)
              └─ If migrations fail → Falls back to create_all()
    ↓
Final Safety Check
    ↓
Verifies all required tables exist
    ↓
Creates any missing tables
    ↓
Creates default admin user (if doesn't exist)

Database File: src/trading_bot.db

docs.title: Docker Development (PostgreSQL)
docs.text:
Database Container: intellecttrader_db (PostgreSQL 15)

Creation: 1. ✅ Docker Compose creates PostgreSQL container 2. ✅ Database intellecttrader created automatically by PostgreSQL 3. ✅ Tables created when app starts (via init_db())

Configuration (docker-compose.yml): 

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: intellecttrader
      POSTGRES_USER: trader
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}

  app:
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy  # Waits for database
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://trader:${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}@db:5432/intellecttrader

Usage: 

docker-compose up

Database Initialization: - App waits for database healthcheck - App starts → init_db() runs → Creates all tables

docs.title: Fresh Database (First Time)
docs.text:
What Happens: 1. init_db() detects no alembic_version table 2. Creates Flask-SQLAlchemy tables: - users - user_credentials - email_tokens - market_data_bars 3. Creates BaseModel tables: - portfolios, positions, orders, trades - portfolio_snapshots - strategies, signals, backtest_results - user_settings, audit_log 4. Creates alembic_version table 5. Stamps database with latest migration revision 6. Creates default admin user (admin@admin.com / admin)

Total Tables Created: 15

docs.title: Existing Database
docs.text: What Happens: 1. init_db() detects alembic_version table exists 2. Runs Alembic migrations: upgrade head 3. Ensures schema is up-to-date 4. If migrations fail → Falls back to create_all() 5. Final safety check verifies all tables exist 6. Creates any missing tables

docs.title: Multiple Layers of Protection
docs.text:
1. Primary: Alembic migrations (command.upgrade())
  2. Secondary: Flask-SQLAlchemy db.create_all()
  3. Tertiary: BaseModel Base.metadata.create_all()
  4. Final: Safety check that verifies each required table exists

Result: Database tables are guaranteed to exist on startup.

docs.title: Default Admin User
docs.text:
Created Automatically (if doesn't exist): - Email: admin@admin.com - Password: admin - Role: owner - Email Verified: True

Location: src/database.py lines 212-225

docs.title: reset-db Command
docs.text:
Command: isbot reset-db

What It Does: 1. Shows warning about data deletion 2. Asks for confirmation (type yes) 3. Calls scripts/reset_db.py 4. reset_db.py: - Uses Alembic migrations to drop all tables - Recreates all tables via migrations - Falls back to create_all() if migrations fail

Usage: 

isbot reset-db
# Type 'yes' when prompted

docs.text:
Test Fresh Database:

isbot stop

rm -f src/trading_bot.db

python -c "

"

docs.title: Email Marketing Deployment Guide
docs.text: This guide describes how to operate the branded marketing email system in production.

docs.title: 1. Database preparation
docs.text:
alembic upgrade head
python scripts/seed_marketing_emails.py

The migration chain creates:

  • email_campaigns – per-campaign cadence and audience rules
  • email_preferences – per-user opt-ins and unsubscribe tokens
  • email_send_logs – audit logs for every send attempt
  • email_events – webhook events (deliveries, opens, bounces)

The seed script ensures that every MarketingCampaignType is present and that all existing users have default preferences.

docs.title: 2. Required environment variables
docs.text: Variable Purpose RESEND_API_KEY Auth token for the Resend API EMAIL_FROM From header used for transactional + marketing emails RESEND_WEBHOOK_SECRET HMAC secret used to validate /api/email/webhooks/resend payloads MARKETING_SCHEDULER_INTERVAL_SECONDS Polling interval for scripts/run_marketing_scheduler.py (defaults to 300 seconds) MARKETING_EMAIL_* / BRAND_* Optional overrides for brand colors, logos, persona, etc.

docs.title: 3. Scheduler process
docs.text:
Add a long-running worker that executes python scripts/run_marketing_scheduler.py with the same env vars as the main web process. Examples:

  • Procfile (Heroku/Railway): 
    web: gunicorn ...
scheduler: python scripts/run_marketing_scheduler.py
  • Docker Compose: 
    marketing_scheduler:
  build: .
  command: python scripts/run_marketing_scheduler.py
  depends_on:
    db:
      condition: service_healthy

docs.title: 4. Webhook wiring
docs.text:
1. In the Resend dashboard, create a webhook pointing to https://<your-domain>/api/email/webhooks/resend.
  2. Copy the signing secret and set RESEND_WEBHOOK_SECRET.
  3. Verify events by sending a test payload—EmailEvent rows should appear and email_send_logs.last_event_type should update.

docs.title: 5. Frontend release
docs.text:
Marketing controls live inside the React frontend. Build the assets prior to deployment:

cd src/frontend
npm install
npm run build

Ship the generated dist directory (already referenced by Flask) alongside the backend release.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:

  • Node 18+
  • Resend API key (for email flows)

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Clone repo & install dependencies (pip install -r requirements.txt, npm install --prefix frontend).
  2. Copy .env.template → .env. Use SQLite by default (no DATABASE_URL).
  3. Start services:
./scripts/isbot.sh start

Frontend will launch on an available Vite port (5173/5174). Backend listens on http://localhost:5002.

docs.title: Useful Commands
docs.text:
./scripts/isbot.sh status       # show running processes and ports
./scripts/isbot.sh logs         # tail backend/frontend logs
./scripts/isbot.sh reset-db     # wipe SQLite (requires confirmation)
./scripts/isbot.sh stop         # stop everything

docs.title: Testing Emails
docs.text: Set RESEND_API_KEY to a test key. Verification and password reset emails are sent via Resend’s sandbox.

docs.title: High-Level Components
docs.text: Layer Description Frontend (Vite + React) Auth pages, dashboard, bot monitor, account settings. Uses Axios with withCredentials. Backend (Flask) REST APIs, Socket.IO, strategy/bot orchestration, encryption. Trading Core Strategies, risk manager, Alpaca service, market data streamer, backtesting engine. Storage SQLite (dev) / PostgreSQL (Railway). SQLAlchemy ORM for models (User, Strategy, Credential, EmailToken).

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
1. Frontend sends login/register requests → backend issues sessions.
  2. Authenticated calls fetch dashboard data (/api/dashboard/data).
  3. When the bot starts, it loads strategies, obtains user-specific Alpaca credentials, streams data, and records trades/logs.
  4. Alpaca REST handles account/positions/orders; Data API/WS fetches bars for strategies.
  5. MarketDataStreamer writes bars to SQLite; DataProvider falls back to cached/Yahoo/AlphaVantage data.
  6. Backtesting engine and documentation share the same strategy/risk modules for consistency.

docs.title: Scripts & Tooling
docs.text:
• scripts/isbot.sh – orchestrates start/stop/restart/status/logs/db reset.
  • scripts/reset_db.py – resets SQLite & recreates tables.
  • GitHub Actions – CI, dependencies, security scans, docs deployment, Railway deployments.

  • API – modular blueprints under src/api/ for future admin/strategy endpoints.

  • SQLite (bundled) or PostgreSQL (for Railway)

docs.title: Initial Steps
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/betintellect-com/trading_bot.git
cd trading_bot
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
npm install --prefix frontend

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Copy .env.template to .env and update:

  • SECRET_KEY, ENCRYPTION_KEY
  • RESEND_API_KEY, EMAIL_FROM
  • Optional OAuth client IDs
  • DATABASE_URL for Postgres (Railway)

docs.title: Running Locally
docs.text:
./scripts/isbot.sh start

This script:

  • Installs frontend deps (first run)
  • Builds/serves Vite
  • Launches Flask with auto-reload
  • Starts Socket.IO and watches logs

docs.title: Python Tests
docs.text:
source venv/bin/activate
pytest
  • Unit tests cover models, utilities, strategies, risk manager, and the Alpaca service.
  • Integration tests (tests/integration) exercise the auth flow end-to-end (registration, verification, password reset).
  • Coverage threshold is enforced via pytest’s --cov settings (fail under 70%).

mypy src/ --ignore-missing-imports --disallow-untyped-defs

All of these run inside .github/workflows/ci.yml as part of the PR gate.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: This guide covers all configuration options for the IntellectScout Trading Bot.

docs.title: Required Variables
docs.text:
# Secret key for Flask sessions (generate with: python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))")
SECRET_KEY=your-secret-key-here

# Encryption key for storing Alpaca credentials (generate with: python -c "from src.utils.encryption import generate_encryption_key; print(generate_encryption_key())")
ENCRYPTION_KEY=your-encryption-key-here

# Database URL
SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI=postgresql://user:password@localhost/trading_bot
# Or for SQLite: sqlite:///trading_bot.db

docs.title: Email Configuration
docs.text:
# Resend API key for sending emails
RESEND_API_KEY=your-resend-api-key

# Email sender address
EMAIL_FROM=noreply@intellectscout.com

# Application URL (for email links)
APP_URL=https://intellectscout.com

docs.title: Trading Configuration
docs.text:
# Default trading symbols (comma-separated)
DEFAULT_TRADING_SYMBOLS=AAPL,MSFT,GOOGL

# Default strategy symbols
DEFAULT_STRATEGY_SYMBOLS=AAPL,MSFT,GOOGL

docs.title: Server Configuration
docs.text:
# Flask port
FLASK_RUN_PORT=5002

# Frontend port
VITE_PORT=5173

# Flask environment
FLASK_ENV=development  # or production

docs.title: Backend Configuration
docs.text: Configuration is managed through: - src/config/constants.py - Application constants - src/config/development.py - Development settings - src/config/staging.py - Staging settings - src/config/production.py - Production settings

docs.title: Frontend Configuration
docs.text: Frontend configuration uses Vite environment variables: - VITE_API_URL - Backend API URL (set at build time)

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Never commit .env files - They contain sensitive credentials
  2. Use strong secret keys - Generate unique keys for each environment
  3. Rotate encryption keys - If compromised, users must re-enter credentials
  4. Use HTTPS in production - Always use SSL/TLS for production deployments

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
FLASK_ENV=development
DEBUG=True
SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI=sqlite:///dev.db

docs.title: Staging
docs.text:
FLASK_ENV=staging
DEBUG=False
SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI=postgresql://user:pass@staging-db/trading_bot

docs.title: Production
docs.text:
FLASK_ENV=production
DEBUG=False
SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI=postgresql://user:pass@prod-db/trading_bot
ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://intellectscout.com

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This guide walks you through spinning up the IntellectScout trading bot with Alpaca’s free tier.

docs.title: 1. Clone & Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/betintellect-com/trading_bot.git
cd trading_bot
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 2. Configure Environment
docs.text:
Copy .env.template to .env and fill in at least:

FLASK_ENV=development
SECRET_KEY=replace-me
ENCRYPTION_KEY=generated-fernet-key
RESEND_API_KEY=your-resend-key
EMAIL_FROM=noreply@intellectscout.com

Leave Alpaca keys blank initially; users enter their own credentials through the UI.

docs.title: 3. Start Services
docs.text:
./scripts/isbot.sh start

This launches:

  • Flask backend on port 5002
  • Vite frontend on whichever port is free (5173/5174)
  • Socket.IO for real-time bot status

docs.title: 4. Register & Verify
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the frontend port.
  2. Register a new account.
  3. Confirm the verification email (Resend).
  4. Sign in and open Account → Alpaca to add your API key/secret (free paper account).

docs.title: 5. Kick Off the Bot
docs.text:
• Configure preferred strategy symbols in Settings.
  • Visit the dashboard; if credentials are verified, start the bot.
  • The bot streams data via Alpaca’s free WebSocket, auto-saves bars, and generates signals.

docs.title: 6. Next Steps
docs.text:
• Review the User Guide for in-depth flows.
  • Explore the Deployment docs to push to Railway.
  • Run the full QA suite: pytest, ruff check ., mypy src/.

docs.title: Profile
docs.text:
• Update display name and avatar (UI avatars) from the profile drawer (coming soon).
  • Email addresses are immutable; use the admin console to change them if needed.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Each user has an encrypted UserCredentials record:

  • Keys are encrypted with the Fernet key supplied via ENCRYPTION_KEY.
  • Verification toggles the is_active field so the bot only uses validated API keys.
  • last_verified_at helps detect stale keys.

docs.title: Roles & Permissions
docs.text:
• trader – default.
  • admin – future management features (viewing user accounts, overriding bots).
  • owner – reserved for the application owner; bootstrapped via init_db.

docs.title: Sessions & Security
docs.text:
• Flask-Session stores sessions server-side; cookies are HTTP-only.
  • CSRF is handled at the API level through JSON requests (no classic form submissions).
  • Rotate the SECRET_KEY and SESSION_KEY_PREFIX for production deployments.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
• Users register via the React frontend.
  • Upon submission, the backend issues a verification token and sends a Resend email.
  • The UI redirects to /verify-email so the user can resend the link or go back to login.

docs.title: Email Verification Flow
docs.text:
1. User clicks the verification link.
  2. Backend validates the token, marks the account as verified, and redirects back to /login?verified=true.
  3. The login page shows a “Email verified” toast.

docs.title: OAuth (Optional)
docs.text: The plan supports future OAuth providers (Google, GitHub, LinkedIn). These endpoints are scaffolded; populate client IDs/secrets through environment variables to enable them.

docs.title: Session Handling
docs.text:
• Flask-Session stores server-side sessions (filesystem in dev, Redis in production).
  • @login_required protects API routes; React uses Axios with withCredentials to keep cookies in sync.
  • The /api/auth/status endpoint powers the frontend auth context.

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text:
1. User clicks “Forgot Password?”.
  2. Backend sends a reset link via Resend.
  3. /reset-password?token=... lets the user set a new password and redirects to login with reset=true.

docs.title: Roles & RBAC
docs.text:
Roles live on the User model (trader, admin, owner).

  • Trader – default; can manage their own Alpaca credentials and run the bot.
  • Admin/Owner – reserved for future management features (multi-user dashboards, team controls).

docs.title: Starting the Bot
docs.text:
• Open the dashboard and ensure Alpaca credentials are verified.
  • Click Start Bot; the server spins up a per-user TradingBot, subscribes to live data, and caches trades/logs.
  • Status messages stream to the Bot Monitor via Socket.IO.

docs.title: Stopping & Restarting
docs.text:
• Use the UI controls or ./scripts/isbot.sh stop to halt all services.
  • The backend caches bot instances per user; stopping frees the streaming task but keeps persisted positions in the database.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
• Dashboard Cards – show equity, buying power, win rate, cumulative PnL.
  • Portfolio Performance Chart – fed by Alpaca’s /account/portfolio/history.
  • Bot Monitor – status feed with informational/warning/error messages emitted by the bot (market closed, API errors, data gaps, etc.).

docs.title: Logs & Alerts
docs.text:
• Structured logs output to console and logs/ (if enabled).
  • Status messages are capped to the latest 100 entries per user to keep the UI responsive.
  • For staging/production, ship logs to a centralized sink (CloudWatch/Logtail) by setting LOG_LEVEL and handler configs.

docs.title: Alpaca Credentials
docs.text:
Each user stores their own Alpaca API key/secret:

  1. Navigate to Account → Alpaca.
  2. Paste key/secret from the Alpaca paper dashboard.
  3. Click Test Connection – this encrypts the credentials, verifies them, and flips the “active” flag.
  4. Once verified, the dashboard/bot gain access to Alpaca REST + WebSocket endpoints.

docs.title: Strategy Selection
docs.text:
Strategies are stored per user in the DB. When no active strategies exist the platform auto-creates:

  • RSI Mean Reversion (per-symbol thresholds)
  • MACD Trend (fast/slow EMA crossovers)
  • Bollinger Bands Reversion

You can manage these entries via the Strategy API (or forthcoming UI) to adjust symbols, thresholds, and timeframes.

docs.title: Risk Configuration
docs.text:
Key parameters live in RiskManager and can be surfaced through settings:

  • risk_per_trade – percent of equity risked per trade (default 1%).
  • max_drawdown – stops the bot when equity drops more than the threshold.
  • max_daily_loss – halts trades for the day if losses exceed the limit.
  • Kelly & ATR sizing automatically use these limits when calculating quantities.

docs.title: Data Streaming & Caching
docs.text:
• Alpaca free WebSocket (IEX) streams bars; MarketDataStreamer saves each bar to SQLite.
  • When Alpaca’s data API lacks access, the DataProvider falls back to cached bars, Yahoo Finance, or Alpha Vantage.
  • The frontend chart pulls from /api/dashboard/data, which now uses Alpaca’s official portfolio history API, so performance charts match real account equity.
